label: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults
statement: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler pigeon.
quote: the characteristic differences which give value to each breed, and which have been accumulated by man’s selection, have not generally first appeared at an early period of life, and have been inherited by the offspring at a corresponding not early period.
scope: domestic breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons

label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
statement: Because the embryo is the animal in a less modified state that partly reveals the structure of its progenitor, two groups that pass through the same or similar embryonic stages are descended from the same or similar parents, however different their adults; this is why embryonic characters are the most valuable for classification.
quote: Thus, community in embryonic structure reveals community of descent.
scope: animal groups, e.g. cirripedes recognised as crustaceans by their larvae

label: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants
statement: Since embryos partly show the structure of less modified ancient progenitors, ancient and extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants, though this may be obscured by early-appearing variations and may be undemonstrable because the geological record does not reach back far enough.
quote: we can clearly see why ancient and extinct forms of life should resemble the embryos of their descendants,—our existing species.
scope: extinct ancestors and the embryos of their living descendants

label: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages
statement: The leading facts of embryology are explained because, in the descendants of a common progenitor, successive slight modifications generally do not appear at a very early period of life (though they may be caused earlier) and are inherited at a corresponding later age, leaving embryos little modified.
quote: the leading facts in embryology, which are second in importance to none in natural history, are explained on the principle of slight modifications not appearing, in the many descendants from some one ancient progenitor, at a very early period in the life of each, though perhaps caused at the earliest, and being inherited at a corresponding not early period.
scope: animals generally

label: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature
statement: Rudimentary, atrophied or aborted organs that bear the stamp of uselessness are extremely common in animals and plants.
quote: Organs or parts in this strange condition, bearing the stamp of inutility, are extremely common throughout nature.
scope: animals and plants generally

label: Rudimentary organs are highly variable
statement: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.
quote: Rudimentary organs in the individuals of the same species are very liable to vary in degree of development and in other respects.
scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants

label: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult
statement: As a universal rule, a rudimentary part is relatively larger compared with adjoining parts in the embryo than in the adult, and some rudiments (such as the teeth of whales and ruminants) appear in the embryo and then wholly disappear.
quote: It is also, I believe, a universal rule, that a rudimentary part or organ is of greater size relatively to the adjoining parts in the embryo, than in the adult
scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants

label: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs
statement: Disuse over successive generations has been the main agency reducing organs to rudiments (as with eyes of cave animals and wings of island birds), aided by natural selection where an organ becomes injurious; because reduction occurs at maturity and is inherited at a corresponding age, rudiments remain relatively larger in the embryo.
quote: I believe that disuse has been the main agency; that it has led in successive generations to the gradual reduction of various organs, until they have become rudimentary
scope: organs reduced under changed habits or conditions, e.g. cave animals and island birds

label: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
statement: Because all members of whole classes are linked by chains of affinities, fossils fill wide gaps between orders, rudiments imply fully developed ancestral organs, and structures within a class share one pattern and similar embryos, descent with modification embraces all members of the same class.
quote: Therefore I cannot doubt that the theory of descent with modification embraces all the members of the same class.
scope: all members of each class of animals and plants

label: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
statement: All animals have descended from at most four or five progenitors, and all plants from an equal or smaller number.
quote: I believe that animals have descended from at most only four or five progenitors, and plants from an equal or lesser number.
scope: all animals and all plants

label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
statement: All living things have much in common in their chemical composition, germinal vesicles, cellular structure, and laws of growth and reproduction, as shown even by the same poison often affecting plants and animals similarly.
quote: Nevertheless all living things have much in common, in their chemical composition, their germinal vesicles, their cellular structure, and their laws of growth and reproduction.
scope: all living organisms

label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
statement: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.
quote: Therefore I should infer from analogy that probably all the organic beings which have ever lived on this earth have descended from some one primordial form, into which life was first breathed.
scope: all organisms that have ever lived on earth

label: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly
statement: The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are known or believed to be connected by intermediate gradations at present, whereas species were connected by them in the past; species should therefore be treated, like genera, as combinations made for convenience.
quote: Hereafter we shall be compelled to acknowledge that the only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed, to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected.
scope: species and varieties of all organisms

label: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change
statement: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.
quote: the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism,—the improvement of one being entailing the improvement or the extermination of others
scope: all organisms over geological time

label: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
statement: Because species are produced and exterminated by slow, still-acting causes, the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations is probably a fair, though imperfect, measure of the time elapsed, and can be used to estimate the length of the blank intervals between formations.
quote: it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time.
scope: fossil faunas and floras of successive formations

label: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history
statement: In early periods of earth's history, when forms of life were fewer and simpler, the rate of organic change was probably slower, and at the first dawn of life it may have been extremely slow.
quote: During early periods of the earth’s history, when the forms of life were probably fewer and simpler, the rate of change was probably slower; and at the first dawn of life, when very few forms of the simplest structure existed, the rate of change may have been slow in an extreme degree.
scope: life on earth across its whole history

label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism
statement: The whole history of the world as known from geology is only a small fragment of the time that has elapsed since the first organism, the progenitor of all later forms, came into existence.
quote: The whole history of the world, as at present known, although of a length quite incomprehensible by us, will hereafter be recognised as a mere fragment of time, compared with the ages which have elapsed since the first creature, the progenitor of innumerable extinct and living descendants, was created.
scope: history of life on earth

label: Every mental power was acquired by gradation
statement: Each mental power and capacity must have been acquired gradually, so psychology will rest on this foundation, and light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.
quote: Psychology will be based on a new foundation, that of the necessary acquirement of each mental power and capacity by gradation.
scope: mental powers of animals, including man

label: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail
statement: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.
quote: We can so far take a prophetic glance into futurity as to foretel that it will be the common and widely-spread species, belonging to the larger and dominant groups, which will ultimately prevail and procreate new and dominant species.
scope: living species and their future descendants (testable retrospectively in the fossil record)

label: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm
statement: Since all living forms are lineal descendants of forms that lived long before the Silurian epoch, the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken and no cataclysm has ever desolated the whole world.
quote: As all the living forms of life are the lineal descendants of those which lived long before the Silurian epoch, we may feel certain that the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken, and that no cataclysm has desolated the whole world.
scope: the history of life on earth

label: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection
statement: Because natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all bodily and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.
quote: And as natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all corporeal and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.
scope: all organisms over long periods

label: The 'entangled bank' laws produce the diversity of living forms
statement: The varied and interdependent forms of life were produced by laws still acting: growth with reproduction; inheritance; variability caused by external conditions and by use and disuse; a rate of increase high enough to cause a struggle for life and so natural selection, which in turn causes divergence of character and extinction of less improved forms.
quote: These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms.
scope: all organic beings

label: Reliance on chance variation and natural selection stalls inquiry into physical causes
statement: As long as fortuitous variation and the survival of the fittest are accepted as sufficient explanations in biology, they will tend to hold back careful investigation of the real physical causes of organic form.
quote: So long and so far as “fortuitous variation” and the “survival of the fittest” remain engrained as fundamental and satisfactory hypotheses in the philosophy of biology, so long will these “satisfactory and specious causes” tend to stay “severe and diligent inquiry,”
scope: explanations of organic form in biology generally

label: Cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves and flowers are shaped by the laws of physics
statement: The material parts of living things (cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves, flowers) are portions of matter whose particles have been moved, moulded and shaped in obedience to the laws of physics.
quote: Cell and tissue, shell and bone, leaf and flower, are so many portions of matter, and it is in obedience to the laws of physics that their particles have been moved, moulded and conformed.
scope: all organisms and their structural parts

label: Problems of organic form are mathematical and problems of growth are physical
statement: The problems of the form of living things are, in the first instance, mathematical problems and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems, so morphology is a branch of physical science.
quote: Their problems of form are in the first instance mathematical problems, and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems; and the morphologist is, _ipso facto_, a student of physical science.
scope: morphology and the study of growth

label: No known physical law is transgressed by the bodily mechanism
statement: However complex living processes are, no physical law (including those of chemistry, surface action and osmosis) is known to be broken by the working of the body.
quote: But all the while, so far as I am aware, no physical law, any more than that of gravity itself, not even among the puzzles of chemical “stereometry,” or of physiological “surface-action” or “osmosis,” is known to be _transgressed_ by the bodily mechanism.
scope: the physical and physiological mechanisms of all organisms

label: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it
statement: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.
quote: In short, the form of an object is a “diagram of forces,” in this sense, at least, that from it we can judge of or deduce the forces that are acting or have acted upon it
scope: living and non-living bodies, including whole organisms and cells

label: Protoplasm behaves as a highly viscous fluid that changes shape under force
statement: The protoplasm of an Amoeba deforms and flows under the slightest pressure, so it is a fluid, but it is far more viscous than water, like treacle, and this viscosity slows its changes of shape.
quote: While the protoplasm of the Amoeba reacts to the slightest pressure, and tends to “flow,” and while we therefore speak of it as a fluid, it is evidently far less mobile than such a fluid, for instance, as water, but is rather like treacle in its slow creeping movements as it changes its shape in response to force.
scope: protoplasm of Amoeba and similar naked cells

label: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form
statement: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.
quote: Like other fluid bodies, its surface, whatsoever other substance, gas, liquid or solid, it be in contact with, and in varying degree according to the nature of that adjacent substance, is the seat of molecular force exhibiting itself as a surface-tension, from the action of which many important consequences follow, which greatly affect the form of the fluid surface.
scope: fluid or semi-fluid cells such as Amoeba

label: Vital phenomena cannot be cleanly divided into physical and non-physical ones
statement: There is no clear rule for deciding what is 'vital', and the properties of organisms cannot be clearly split into those of physical origin and those peculiar to living things, so physical analysis must proceed piece by piece.
quote: it is plain that we have no clear rule or guide as to what is “vital” and what is not; the whole assemblage of so-called vital phenomena, or properties of the organism, cannot be clearly classified into those that are physical in origin and those that are _sui generis_ and peculiar to living things.
scope: properties and processes of living organisms

label: Nuclei, chromosomes and germ-plasm act only as seats of energy and centres of force
statement: In development, variation and inheritance, material elements such as the spermatozoon, nucleus, chromosomes or germ-plasm never act as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and centres of force.
quote: we must most carefully realise in the outset that the spermatozoon, the nucleus, the chromosomes or the germ-plasm can never _act_ as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and as centres of force.
scope: embryology and heredity

label: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
statement: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.
quote: then the value of _k_, according to whether it varies or remains constant, will tell us at once whether there has or has not been a tendency to gradual alteration in the general form.
scope: fishes and other growing animals of roughly constant density

label: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
statement: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.
quote: But in a terrestrial animal the weight which tends to crush its limbs or which its muscles have to move, varies as the cube of its linear dimensions; and so, to the possible magnitude of an animal, living under the direct action of gravity, there is a definite limit set.
scope: terrestrial animals, especially large mammals

label: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals
statement: An animal wholly immersed in water whose density about matches the water, like a whale, has its weight counterpoised, so there is no longer a physical barrier to its indefinite growth in size.
quote: Under these circumstances there is no longer a physical barrier to the indefinite growth in magnitude of the animal.
scope: fully aquatic animals of near-neutral buoyancy, e.g. whales

label: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
statement: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).
quote: In general, as Greenhill shews, the diameter of a homogeneous body must increase as the power 3/2 of the height, which accounts for the slender proportions of young trees, compared with the stunted appearance of old and large ones.
scope: trees and other tall self-supporting plant stems

label: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly
statement: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.
quote: the singular result ought to follow that, in swimming for instance, the larger fish ought to be able to put on a spurt of speed far in excess of the smaller one; but the distance travelled by the year’s end should be very much alike for both of them.
scope: similar, closely related animals of different size, especially swimming fish

label: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3
statement: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).
quote: The work requiring to be done, then, varies as the power 3½ of the bird’s linear dimensions, while the work of which the bird is capable depends on the mass of its muscles, and therefore varies as the cube of its linear dimensions.
scope: flying birds of similar proportions

label: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible
statement: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.
quote: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.
scope: large birds, including ratites

label: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere
statement: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.
quote: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.
scope: Carboniferous giant insects and Jurassic pterosaurs

label: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size
statement: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.
quote: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.
scope: jumping animals of similar construction across sizes, from fleas to horses

label: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking
statement: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.
quote: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.
scope: swimming, flying and walking animals of similar construction

label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like
statement: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.
quote: Were the force of gravity to be doubled, our bipedal form would be a failure, and the majority of terrestrial animals would resemble short-legged saurians, or else serpents.
scope: terrestrial animals

label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass
statement: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
quote: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.
scope: internal surfaces of animals, e.g. gut lining and brain cortex

label: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres
statement: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.
quote: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension
scope: small organisms and individual cells versus large animals

label: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones
statement: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.
quote: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.
scope: large multicellular organisms versus small organisms and individual cells

label: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass
statement: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.
quote: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.
scope: dividing cells, including cleaving eggs

label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
statement: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.
quote: An immediate and remarkable result of the principles just described is a tendency on the part of all cells, according to their kind, to vary but little about a certain mean size, and to have, in fact, certain absolute limitations of magnitude.
scope: tissue cells of animals, compared across individuals of different body size

label: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells
statement: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.
quote: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.
scope: nerve cells and ganglia across animal species

label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
statement: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.
quote: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.
scope: the smallest micro-organisms

label: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions
statement: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.
quote: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.
scope: all organisms except very minute ones (e.g. single small cells shaped by surface tension)

label: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development
statement: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.
quote: It may sometimes be a very _constant_ one, in which case the organism, while growing in bulk, suffers little or no perceptible change in form; but such equilibrium seldom endures for more than a season, and when the _ratio_ tends to alter, then we have the phenomenon of morphological “development,” or steady and persistent change of form.
scope: growing multicellular organisms

label: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet
statement: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.
quote: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.
scope: vertebrate embryos (blastoderm / germinal disc), especially the chick

label: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young
statement: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal stages.
quote: it is accordingly obvious that in any two related individuals (whether specifically identical or not) the differences between them must manifest themselves gradually, and be but little apparent in the young. It is for the same simple reason that animals which are of very different sizes when adult, differ less and less in size (as well as in form) as we trace them backwards through the foetal stages.
scope: related individuals and species, especially mammals with foetal development

label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
statement: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.
quote: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”
scope: humans, birth to adulthood

label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
statement: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.
quote: We should see that a man’s full stature endures but for a spell; long before fifty it has begun to abate, by sixty it is notably lessened, in extreme old age the old man’s frame is shrunken and it is but a memory that “he once was tall.”
scope: adult humans

label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
statement: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.
quote: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.
scope: growing humans (and organisms generally)

label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
statement: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
quote: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
scope: humans, childhood and adolescence

label: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
statement: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
quote: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.
scope: animals generally

label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
statement: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
quote: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
scope: cold-blooded animals, especially fishes

label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
statement: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
quote: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.
scope: animals, especially mammals

label: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
statement: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
quote: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
scope: human foetus

label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
statement: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.
quote: Just as the human curve of growth has its slight but well-marked interruptions, or variations in rate, coinciding with such epochs as birth and puberty, so is it with other animals, and this phenomenon is particularly striking in the case of animals which undergo a regular metamorphosis.
scope: animals, including man, mouse, silkworm, tadpole

label: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight
statement: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.
quote: The negative growth, or actual loss of bulk and weight which often, and perhaps always, accompanies metamorphosis, is well shewn in the case of the eel.
scope: animals with metamorphosis (insects, amphibians, eels)

label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
statement: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
scope: humans, childhood and adolescence

label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
statement: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.
quote: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.
scope: multicellular organisms

label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
statement: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.
quote: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain
scope: humans and other vertebrates (lion, dogfish)

label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
statement: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
quote: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
scope: plaice (and by extension other fishes)

label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
statement: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
scope: plaice and similar seasonally spawning fishes

label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
statement: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
quote: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.
scope: growth and development of plants and animals within normal temperature limits

label: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage
statement: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.
quote: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.
scope: physiological processes, especially growth, in plants and animals

label: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C
statement: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.
quote: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day
scope: temperate and warm-climate plants (root and shoot elongation)

label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
statement: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
scope: fishes (plaice, haddock) and humans

label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
statement: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
scope: Arizona climate, 1390s–1910s, inferred from ponderosa (yellow) pine rings

label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
statement: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.
quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells, as well as on the actual amount of chemical metabolism performed by them
scope: growing cells of plants and animals, especially plant elongation and early embryos

label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
statement: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
scope: brine-shrimps (Artemia) in waters of varying salinity
